## Theoretical Foundations & Methodological Overview

Standard Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression relies on the fundamental assumption that observational units are independent and identically distributed ($e_i \sim \text{i.i.d.}$). In international relations, comparative political economy, and global public health, this assumption of independence rarely holds true. Observational units do not exist in geographic isolation; rather, they interact across administrative boundaries through physical proximity, bilateral trade flows, migration channels, shared ecosystems, and policy contagion.

As Waldo Tobler articulated in his First Law of Geography: *"Everything is related to everything else, but near things are more related than distant things."*

When analyzing cross-sectional public health indicators such as national life expectancy, ignoring spatial dependence introduces three major theoretical and econometric vulnerabilities:

1. **Spatial Autocorrelation**: Unobserved exogenous shocks (e.g., epidemic outbreaks, climate shocks, regional conflicts) spill across national borders, causing regression residuals to cluster geographically.

2. **Standard Error Bias**: Treating spatially dependent nations as independent overestimates the effective sample size (N), suppressing standard errors and inflating t-statistics.

3. **Substantive Misspecification**: Ignoring neighborhood context fails to capture how policy interventions or health dynamics in adjacent states directly impact domestic outcomes.

### Learning Objectives

By completing this analytical workbook, you will develop competence in:

- Executing spatial joins between cross-sectional attribute data and vector boundary polygons using `sf` and `rnaturalearth`.
- Constructing spatial neighbor linkages and row-standardized spatial weight matrices (W) using `spdep`.
- Calculating spatial lag variables (Wy) to systematically quantify neighborhood context effects.
- Running Global Moran's I hypothesis tests to evaluate global spatial autocorrelation.
- Deriving and mapping Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) to detect statistically significant health hotspots, coldspots, and spatial outliers.

## Module 1: Dynamic Data Path Resolution & Spatial Ingestion

To model spatial clustering across global economies, we load cross-sectional life expectancy records from Our World in Data (OWID) for 2019 and join them with vector boundary polygons from Natural Earth using ISO 3-letter country codes (`iso_a3`).

```{r}
# Dynamic Path Resolution for execution flexibility across root or /reports working directories
possible_paths <- c(
  "data/life_expectancy_data.csv",
  "../data/life_expectancy_data.csv",
  "/Users/yawdgyal/Desktop/R for github/Spatial Econometrics & Geographic Clustering/data/life_expectancy_data.csv"
)

data_path <- possible_paths[file.exists(possible_paths)][1]

if (is.na(data_path)) {
  stop("Could not locate 'life_expectancy_data.csv'. Please verify it exists in your project's data/ folder.")
}

# Ingest raw OWID panel dataset
owid_raw <- read_csv(data_path)

# Standardize column names and filter to 2019 cross-section
owid_2019 <- owid_raw %>%
  rename(
    country  = Entity,
    code     = Code,
    year     = Year,
    life_exp = `Life expectancy`
  ) %>%
  filter(year == 2019, !is.na(code)) %>%
  select(code, country, life_exp)

# Fetch spatial geometries from Natural Earth
world_polygons <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") %>%
  select(iso_a3, name, continent, geometry) %>%
  filter(continent != "Antarctica")

# Join attribute data with vector boundaries on ISO 3-letter codes
spatial_df <- world_polygons %>%
  inner_join(owid_2019, by = c("iso_a3" = "code")) %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(geometry))

head(spatial_df)
```

## Module 2: Cartographic & Distributional Visualizations

Choropleth mapping and distribution plots allow us to visually examine continuous geographic gradients and regional health variations across global continents.

```{r}
fig1 <- ggplot(data = spatial_df) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = life_exp), color = "white", size = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma", 
    name = "Life Exp.\n(Years)",
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 1: Global Distribution of National Life Expectancy (2019)",
    subtitle = "Continuous Spatial Projection Illustrating Global Health Disparities",
    caption = "Source: Our World in Data & Natural Earth"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.key.width = unit(2, "cm"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )

print(fig1)
```

```{r}
fig2 <- ggplot(spatial_df, aes(x = reorder(continent, life_exp, FUN = median), y = life_exp, fill = continent)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, color = NA) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5, color = "grey20") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 2: Continental Distribution & Intra-Regional Variance",
    subtitle = "Violin and Boxplot Decompositions of Health Metrics (2019)",
    x = "Continent",
    y = "Life Expectancy at Birth (Years)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )

print(fig2)
```

## Module 3: Spatial Weight Matrices (W) & Spatial Lag Construction

To quantify spatial dependencies, we define neighbor linkages using a **Queen Contiguity Matrix** (units sharing a boundary edge or vertex) and apply **Row Standardization** (`style = "W"`).

The spatial lag ($Wy_i$) computes the weighted average life expectancy of nation $i$'s immediate geographic neighbors:

$$
\text{Spatial Lag}_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{ij} y_j \quad \text{where} \quad \sum_{j=1}^{N} w_{ij} = 1
$$

```{r}
# Spatial Weight Matrix & Spatial Lag Construction
neighbors_list <- poly2nb(spatial_df, queen = TRUE)
spatial_weights <- nb2listw(neighbors_list, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

spatial_df$spatial_lag_life_exp <- lag.listw(spatial_weights, spatial_df$life_exp, zero.policy = TRUE)

spatial_df <- spatial_df %>%
  mutate(
    scale_life_exp = scale(life_exp)[,1],
    scale_lag_life_exp = scale(spatial_lag_life_exp)[,1]
  )
```

### Global Moran's Scatterplot

Plotting a country's standardized life expectancy ($Zy_i$) against its neighborhood's standardized spatial lag ($ZWy_i$) yields a **Moran Scatterplot**. The slope of the regression trendline corresponds directly to the Global Moran's I coefficient.

```{r}
fig3 <- ggplot(spatial_df, aes(x = scale_life_exp, y = scale_lag_life_exp)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, size = 2.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "firebrick", se = TRUE) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 3: Global Moran's Scatterplot of Health Metrics",
    subtitle = "Slope Equals the Global Moran's I Spatial Autocorrelation Coefficient",
    x = "Standardized National Life Expectancy (Z-Score)",
    y = "Standardized Spatial Lag / Neighbor Average (Z-Score)"
  ) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13))

print(fig3)
```

## Module 4: Autocorrelation Testing & LISA Diagnostics

### Global Moran's I Test

We execute a formal Global Moran's I hypothesis test to determine whether global health metrics display statistically significant spatial clustering ($I > 0$), dispersion ($I < 0$), or randomness ($I \approx 0$).

```{r}
moran_global <- moran.test(spatial_df$life_exp, listw = spatial_weights, zero.policy = TRUE)
print(moran_global)
```

### Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)

While Global Moran's I provides a single index for the entire globe, Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) identify localized spatial clusters:

- **High-High (Hotspot)**: High life expectancy nation surrounded by high life expectancy neighbors.
- **Low-Low (Coldspot)**: Low life expectancy nation surrounded by low life expectancy neighbors.
- **Low-High / High-Low (Spatial Outliers)**: Nations whose outcomes significantly deviate from their surroundings.

```{r}
lisa_results <- localmoran(spatial_df$life_exp, listw = spatial_weights, zero.policy = TRUE)

spatial_df <- spatial_df %>%
  mutate(
    local_moran_i = lisa_results[, "Ii"],
    lisa_p_value  = lisa_results[, "Pr(z != E(Ii))"],
    quadrant = case_when(
      scale_life_exp > 0 & scale_lag_life_exp > 0 ~ "High-High",
      scale_life_exp < 0 & scale_lag_life_exp < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      scale_life_exp < 0 & scale_lag_life_exp > 0 ~ "Low-High",
      scale_life_exp > 0 & scale_lag_life_exp < 0 ~ "High-Low",
      TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
    ),
    cluster_category = if_else(lisa_p_value < 0.05, quadrant, "Not Significant")
  )
```

```{r}
lisa_colors <- c(
  "High-High"       = "#d7191c",
  "Low-Low"         = "#2b83ba",
  "Low-High"        = "#fdae61",
  "High-Low"        = "#abdda4",
  "Not Significant" = "grey85"
)

fig4 <- ggplot(data = spatial_df) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cluster_category), color = "white", size = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = lisa_colors, name = "LISA Cluster Type\n(p < 0.05)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 4: Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) Cluster Map",
    subtitle = "Statistically Significant Health Hotspots (High-High) & Coldspots (Low-Low)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )

print(fig4)
```

```{r}
fig5 <- ggplot(spatial_df, aes(x = continent, y = local_moran_i, fill = continent)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = 21, outlier.fill = "red") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set3") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 5: Magnitude of Local Spatial Clustering Across Continents",
    subtitle = "Higher Positive Local Moran Statistics Indicate Stronger Local Spatial Dependence",
    x = "Continent",
    y = "Local Moran's I Statistic (Ii)"
  ) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 13)
  )

print(fig5)
```

## Student Coding Lab Exercises

Complete these exercises in your R environment to practice your spatial analytics pipeline.

### Exercise 1: Extract Significant Cluster Lists

Write a `dplyr` pipeline using `spatial_df` to display all countries identified as statistically significant **High-High** hotspots or **Low-Low** coldspots ($p < 0.05$), arranged by life expectancy.

```{r}
# EXERCISE 1: Extract significant LISA clusters
significant_clusters <- spatial_df %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(lisa_p_value < 0.05, cluster_category %in% c("High-High", "Low-Low")) %>%
  select(country, continent, life_exp, cluster_category, lisa_p_value) %>%
  arrange(cluster_category, desc(life_exp))

head(significant_clusters, 10)
```

### Exercise 2: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN = 4) Sensitivity Analysis

Re-calculate spatial weight matrices using a **K-Nearest Neighbors** specification ($k = 4$) via `knearneigh()` and `knn2nb()` to evaluate how forcing island nations to possess 4 spatial neighbors alters Global Moran's I.

```{r}
# EXERCISE 2: KNN Spatial Weight Matrix
coords <- st_centroid(st_geometry(spatial_df))
knn_neighbors <- knearneigh(coords, k = 4)
knn_nb <- knn2nb(knn_neighbors)
knn_weights <- nb2listw(knn_nb, style = "W")

knn_moran_test <- moran.test(spatial_df$life_exp, listw = knn_weights, zero.policy = TRUE)
knn_moran_test
```

### Exercise 3: Distance-Based Spatial Weights

Construct a distance-threshold spatial weight matrix using `dnearneigh()` and execute a Global Moran's I test to evaluate distance decay effects across sovereign states.

```{r}
# EXERCISE 3: Distance-threshold spatial weight matrix
max_dist <- max(unlist(nbdists(poly2nb(spatial_df, queen = TRUE), coords)))
dist_nb <- dnearneigh(coords, d1 = 0, d2 = max_dist)
dist_weights <- nb2listw(dist_nb, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

moran.test(spatial_df$life_exp, listw = dist_weights, zero.policy = TRUE)
```

### Exercise 4: Identifying Spatial Outliers

Write a `dplyr` pipeline to isolate and display all statistically significant spatial outliers (**High-Low** and **Low-High** cases) where national health outcomes sharply diverge from neighboring trends.

```{r}
# EXERCISE 4: Filter spatial outliers
spatial_outliers <- spatial_df %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(lisa_p_value < 0.05, cluster_category %in% c("High-Low", "Low-High")) %>%
  select(country, continent, life_exp, spatial_lag_life_exp, cluster_category, lisa_p_value)

spatial_outliers
```
